displayQuote: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation

meta.title: Who really said "The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Thoreau wrote it in Walden (1854), Chapter 1, the “Economy” chapter. But the popular tail “go to the grave with the song still in them” is not his.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Thoreau — from Walden (1854), the “Economy” chapter. The added “song still in them” ending, though, was never his.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Thoreau wrote this in ‘‘Walden’’ (1854), in the opening chapter “Economy.” The line is confirmed word-for-word in the book’s ninth paragraph; only the widely-tacked-on ending — “and go to the grave with the song still in them” — is not Thoreau’s.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Walden; or, Life in the Woods

source.excerpt: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. What is called resignation is confirmed desperation. From the desperate city you go into the desperate country, and have to console yourself with the bravery of minks and muskrats. A stereotyped but unconscious despair is concealed even under what are called the games and amusements of mankind. There is no play in them, for this comes after work. But it is a characteristic of wisdom not to do desperate things.
trail: The line is Thoreau’s own: it opens paragraph 9 of “Economy,” confirmed in the Readers’ Thoreau edition of Walden ↗.
‘‘Walden’’ was published 9 August 1854 by Ticknor & Fields; the “Economy” chapter ↗ carries the passage in full.
The Walden Woods Project’s mis-quotation page ↗ confirms the sentence is genuine but flags the added “song still in them” tail as not Thoreau’s.
source.cutTag: ↑ the famous line opens a longer, darker paragraph
source.excerptNote: The single sentence is almost always quoted alone; in ‘‘Walden’’ it opens a sustained meditation on resignation and unconscious despair.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, poet and naturalist, and a leading figure of New England Transcendentalism. In 1845 he moved to a small cabin he built beside Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts; the book that grew out of that two-year experiment, Walden; or, Life in the Woods (1854), is his most famous work. He also wrote the influential essay Civil Disobedience (1849).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The sentence itself is authentically Thoreau. The misattribution problem is what people add to it: a sentimental ending Thoreau never wrote.

items.who: “… and go to the grave with the song still in them”
items.why: This uplifting tail is routinely appended to Thoreau’s line but appears nowhere in ‘‘Walden’’. The Walden Woods Project ↗ flags it as not Thoreau’s, suggesting it echoes Oliver Wendell Holmes’s poem “The Voiceless” (“Alas for those that never sing, / But die with all their music in them”).

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine line is a single sentence in the “Economy” chapter of ‘‘Walden’’; the “song still in them” ending is a later graft, per the Walden Woods Project ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thoreau opens ‘‘Walden’’ with a long critique of how his neighbours live — overworked, indebted, and resigned. “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation” is the hinge of that argument: not a lament but a diagnosis, offered so that readers might choose a more deliberate life.

The book is usually read as an answer to its own gloomiest sentence. Thoreau’s two years at the pond are presented as evidence that the “desperation” is not fate but habit, and that simplicity and attention can dissolve it.
context.pull: “It is a characteristic of wisdom not to do desperate things.”
